If you only remember one thing: Anthropic is heading to the stock market as soon as next week, at a possible valuation of about one point four trillion dollars. And it just launched an office suite aimed straight at Microsoft.

Number one. Anthropic's big week.
On Tuesday, Anthropic launched a set of office tools. Claude Meetings, starting with Google Meet. Claude Whiteboards and Claude Sheets, both in beta. And Claude Data, formerly called Dashboards. Its connectors reach more than nine thousand apps, like Salesforce and Workday. Microsoft shares fell more than two percent after the news.
On the I P O: the target price is seventy to seventy eight dollars a share. Trading could start around November nineteenth.
Your Rundown leads with Anthropic saying "pacing, not pausing" with its new model, Fable five point two. Fortune notes the new models are priced below OpenAI's G P T six Astra.
And Tech Policy Press asks a provocative question: could the United States seize Anthropic at a discount?
Why it matters: A I labs are moving from chatbots into the everyday tools of office work. And into public markets, where the scrutiny gets much sharper.

Number two. The Nvidia spy scandal and chip controls.
Nvidia's board opened an inquiry into C E O Jensen Huang's relationship with Alice Huang, a former executive at Megaspeed. The New York Times and the Financial Times, citing unnamed U S intelligence officials, reported she was a Chinese intelligence agent. China denies it. The F B I is reportedly investigating. President Trump said he doesn't think Huang needs to worry.
In Congress, Senators Elizabeth Warren and Jim Banks are pushing the A I Overwatch Act. Representative Bill Foster is pushing the Chip Security Act. Reports point to tighter export curbs. One research group, Epoch A I, estimates chips equal to about one point six million H one hundreds reached China in violation of the rules through the end of last year.
Also from your Recode China A I newsletter: how Ulanqab, a farming city in Inner Mongolia, became an A I computing boomtown that draws young workers.
Why it matters: one personal scandal is now giving lawmakers momentum for the toughest chip export rules yet.

Number three. A I policy.
Scott Wiener won Nancy Pelosi's open San Francisco seat in the House. He's positioned to shape federal A I policy.
From your E U A I Act newsletter: the E U's A I Office is proposing rules for independent outside evaluators of the most powerful A I models. Analysts flag gaps in testing capacity and incident reporting.
Australia is considering criminal penalties for rogue A I companies. And two U S towns voted to ban Flock surveillance cameras.
Tech Policy Press also has Daphne Keller's close read of the TikTok and Meta teen safety settlements.
Why it matters: who gets to test A I, and who is liable when it fails, is becoming the core policy fight on both sides of the Atlantic.

Number four. A I and the wider world.
From your A I Collective newsletter: identity and provenance. Proving who an A I agent is, and what it's allowed to do, is the missing foundation of the agent-driven internet.
And for your comms brain: The Substack Post shared an excerpt from a new book, How to Save the Media, out November seventeenth.
Why it matters: as agents act on our behalf, trust and verification become a communications problem, not just an engineering one.

Number five. Tech for good.
The A I for Good summit, run by the U N's telecom agency, revealed its first speakers for twenty twenty seven, and opened a new prize challenge.
Aid groups keep making the case for putting data safeguards first when using A I. The International Rescue Committee's Signpost program, a good example, has now served more than twenty million people in thirty countries.
Why it matters: the best humanitarian A I pairs reach with real protection for vulnerable people's data.

Also in your Reads. The New Yorker, on a Russian filmmaker upsetting the Kremlin, and what it would take to change our relationship with technology. Noosphere, on what's next for the Republican party and J D Vance after the midterms. Glasp, on what stays human when A I outpaces us. And GalleriesNow, with the week in art.

The thread today: A I is now big enough to be a public company, a national security issue, and a regulated industry, all at once.

That's your briefing. Have a great Wednesday, Sin.
